title: USPS Publishes Final Rule to Restrict Mail-In Voting Despite Court Orders Blocking It
excerpt: The Postal Service released a 95-page regulation that would let it refuse to deliver ballots in noncompliant states, positioning the rule to take effect the moment a court lifts existing injunctions.
body:
• The U.S. Postal Service published a final 95-page rule Friday to tighten requirements for mail-in voting ahead of the November 2026 congressional elections.
  • A federal judge has already blocked the rule from taking effect, but USPS issued it so it can be implemented immediately if courts lift their injunctions.
  • Under the rule, USPS would refuse to deliver ballots in states that do not submit voter participation lists and comply with new envelope and barcode standards.
  • Twenty-four state attorneys general have formally opposed the regulation as an unconstitutional federal power grab over state-run elections.

The U.S. Postal Service published a final rule late Friday to tighten requirements for mail-in voting ahead of November's congressional elections, even as a federal court order blocks the changes from taking effect.

USPS said it was issuing the 95-page regulation so it could take immediate effect if a court lifted the injunctions against it. Under the rule, the Postal Service would not accept ballots for delivery in states that fail to comply with its new standards — effectively giving the federal mail carrier the power to decide whose ballots it will carry.

What the Rule Requires

The regulation traces back to President Trump's March 2026 Executive Order 14399, titled "Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections." The order directed USPS to write a rule under which it "shall not transmit" a mail-in or absentee ballot unless the voter has been enrolled on a state-specific Mail-In and Absentee Participation List.

https://x.com/stephen_richer/status/2090991054883364984

Under the final rule, each state would provide USPS with voter lists at least 30 days before ballots are mailed. When election offices bring outbound ballots to the Postal Service, USPS would check the mailing against the list before accepting it, turning back any addressed to voters not on the roster. The rule also mandates new envelope designs bearing the Official Election Mail logo and unique Intelligent Mail barcodes to track which voters received and returned ballots.

"We would tell the state that we need the manifest," Postmaster General David Steiner told the Senate in June when asked whether the agency would deliver ballots for noncompliant states.

Courts Have Pushed Back

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston blocked the administration from implementing the executive order in a ruling on August 11, expanding on an earlier June order that covered 23 mostly Democratic-led states. In granting a nationwide injunction, Talwani wrote that the executive branch has no constitutional authority to regulate elections — a responsibility the Constitution assigns to individual states.

"The [executive order] is presently causing confusion and threatening both increasing chaos and an erosion of trust in our democracy."

— Judge Indira Talwani, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

Republican-led states have appealed the nationwide halt. Meanwhile, 24 state attorneys general — from California to New York to North Carolina — filed formal comments calling the proposed rule unconstitutional and warning it would "create confusion, chaos, and distrust in state election systems."

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Mail-in voting is widely used by Indian Americans, particularly dual-income families and elderly voters who depend on absentee ballots in states like California, Texas, New Jersey, and Illinois. Any disruption to mail ballot delivery could disproportionately affect communities that rely on it for access, especially in the November 2026 midterms where several competitive House and Senate races are in play.

What's Next

The final rule's practical impact hinges entirely on whether appellate courts overturn the existing injunctions. If the block holds, USPS will be barred from implementing the regulation for the 2026 elections. If a court lifts it, the rule takes effect immediately — potentially upending ballot delivery in states that have not submitted voter lists.

Neither the White House nor the Justice Department responded to requests for comment on the rule's publication.
nri_angle: Indian Americans in key states rely heavily on mail-in voting; any ballot delivery disruption could disproportionately affect diaspora voter access in the 2026 midterms.
